bib.title: A Survey of Frontiers in LLM Reasoning: Inference Scaling, Learning to Reason, and Agentic Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Survey of Frontiers in LLM Reasoning: Inference Scaling, Learning to Reason, and Agentic Systems", Zixuan Ke, Fangkai Jiao, Yifei Ming, Xuan-Phi Nguyen, Austin Xu, Do Xuan Long, Minzhi Li, Chengwei Qin, Peifeng Wang, Silvio Savarese, Caiming Xiong, Shafiq Joty (Salesforce AI Research, NUS, NTU and others). Preprint arXiv:2504.09037v4, 17 Mar 2026.

COVERAGE: 75 of 75 pages extracted (306,852 chars). I read pp.1-39 in full (abstract through conclusion). That includes every table and equation. The paper has no appendix and no results tables. I skimmed pp.40-75 (acknowledgements and references only) for origins. Figures 1-6 were checked through the caption script. The text file is at /tmp/ke_out/t.txt, with [[pN]] page markers.

NATURE OF THE SOURCE: this is a taxonomy survey. It reports almost no benchmark results of its own. Nearly every number below is a number the survey relays from another paper. Cite the underlying papers for these, not the survey, unless you only want the taxonomy.

BEST-FIT NOTE: 04-multi-agent-design-patterns.md is the best fit. Its "When self-critique helps, and when it doesn't" section matches the survey's generator-evaluator and generator-critic-refiner patterns, the over-refinement warning, the debate and reconcile patterns, and the self-refinement-fails-without-a-verifier evidence. Second fit: 01-agent-fundamentals.md, for "How agents learn" (SFT, RL, GRPO, learning to reason) and the interactiveness/autonomy definition of an agent. Weak fit: 02-tool-use-and-react.md, for ReAct, LATS and tool use as an inference-scaling action (the paragraph is short). I did not open note 04 in full or check its existing citations. The caller should check whether it already cites this paper.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The survey sorts reasoning methods on two axes. Regime is inference scaling versus learning to reason. Architecture is standalone LLM, single-agent or multi-agent. Each cell is split into input (prompt, perception, communication) and output (selection, action, coordination).
  number: none
  setup: taxonomy, Fig. 2/3
  quote: "we categorize existing research into two orthogonal dimensions:(1) Regime, refers to whether reasoning is achieved through inference-time strategies (aka. inference-time"
  where: p.2

- A system has three components: reasoner (policy), verifier (reward function) and refiner. One LLM can play all three, as in self-refinement.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2.2, Fig 4
  quote: "(a) A Reasonerthat generates the reasoning steps, serving as the policy model; (b) Verifiersthat evaluate the correctness of the final outcome and/or reasoning steps, serving as reward functions; and (c) A Refinerthat improves reasoning trajectories"
  where: p.8

- An agent differs from a standalone LLM by interactiveness and autonomy. Agentic-ness is a spectrum (credited to Kapoor et al. 2024). Single-agent means agent-environment interaction. Multi-agent adds agent-agent communication. The environment is whatever the agent cannot modify, so an LLM judge or verifier counts as environment.
  number: none
  setup: definitions, Sec 2.3.2
  quote: "The more interactiveness and autonomy an LLM exhibits, the more agentic it is considered to be."
  where: p.11

- Generator-evaluator pattern: verifiers help, but the generator can reward-hack them. Quoted from the survey, citing Kim et al. 2024d.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2.3.3
  quote: "Kim et al. (2024d) points out that verifiers are vulnerable to reward hacking, where the reasoner exploits loopholes in the verifier to achieve higher reward scores, ultimately degrading the overall performance of the agentic system."
  where: p.11

- Generator-critic-refiner pattern: it risks over-refinement (Chen et al. 2024b), where extra iterations give diminishing or negative returns.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2.3.3
  quote: "it may also lead to a phenomenon known as ‘over-refinement’ (Chen et al., 2024b), where the agent iterates excessively, leading to diminishing returns or even degraded performance rather than improvement."
  where: p.11

- Self-refinement is unreliable without a robust verifier. Some studies show success; others (Stechly 2023/2024, Huang 2024a, Valmeekam 2023, Shridhar 2024) show poor performance. Verifiers also pass false positives, which erodes the return on extra inference compute.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2.1, survey of the literature
  quote: "others highlight poor performance in the absence of robust verifiers (Stechly et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024a; Stechly et al., 2024; Valmeekam et al., 2023; Shridhar et al., 2024)."
  where: p.17

- LLM-as-judge generally underperforms trained reward models at verification. Generative reward models are the hybrid.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2.1, citing Zhang et al. 2024e
  quote: "recent studies have found that LLM-as-judge models generally underperform reward models (RMs) in terms of verification (Zhang et al., 2024e)."
  where: p.17

- Process reward models (PRMs) generally beat outcome reward models (ORMs) as inference-time verifiers. In RL training the picture is mixed: Shao 2024 and Havrilla 2024 saw small gains from a PRM, and others saw significant gains. Outcome-only supervision may reward wrong chains that reach right answers.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2.1, 4.2.2, 5.2.2
  quote: "PRMs generally yield greater improvements during inference compared to ORMs (Uesato et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2024)."
  where: p.17

- Automatic PRM labels come from rollouts. The worked example gives 0.6 confidence for a step when 3 of 5 completions are correct. Such labels do not generalize beyond the sampling policy.
  number: 0.6 (3 of 5 rollouts)
  setup: MCTS-style step labelling
  quote: "suppose we roll out five completions randomly from the same prefixy ≤t, with three rollouts arriving at the correct answer. Then, the confidence that the prefixy≤t is correct can be approximated as 0.6."
  where: p.24

- Small models need stronger models as step verifiers (Zhang et al. 2024i).
  number: ≤13B parameters
  setup: intermediate-step verification
  quote: "smaller models (≤13B parameters) in particular need stronger models acting as verifiers to validate and correct intermediate steps."
  where: p.16

- Self-consistency branches only at the start of the chain and has limited diversity. Tree, Graph and Forest of Thoughts branch at finer grain. Aggregation is by ensemble (majority vote, confidence) or by verifier.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.1.2
  quote: "Early methods, such as self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023f), introduced branching only at the beginning of the reasoning chain"
  where: p.16

- Inference-time compute can beat parameter scaling (Snell et al. 2024). The survey also quotes the OpenAI o1 line that performance "consistently improves with more reinforcement learning (train-time compute) and with more time spent thinking (test-time compute)".
  number: none
  setup: relayed claim, no setup given in the survey
  quote: "optimal scaling of test-time compute can be more effective than scaling model parameters (Snell et al., 2024)"
  where: p.3, p.13

- DeepSeek-R1 and GRPO: pure RL with verifiable outcome rewards. GRPO drops PPO's value model and uses the group-normalized reward as advantage. R1 treats the whole response as one action (a one-step MDP). DAPO fixes length bias in GRPO. The survey says reflection and exploration of alternatives emerged spontaneously under RL.
  number: none (equation 7)
  setup: Sec 4.1.2
  quote: "AGRPO(si,t,ai,t) =A GRPO(oi) = ri−mean(R)std(R) ."
  where: p.22

- Small curated SFT sets match large ones (figures relayed from the cited papers). Muennighoff 2025 used 1,000 samples on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and surpassed o1-preview on competition math. Ye 2025 used 817 samples, and the gain required a strong base model. SFT replications of o1 used 4K-20K samples. Xu 2025e scaled to 1M CoT samples with diminishing returns.
  number: 1,000 samples; 817 samples; 4K-20K; 1 million
  setup: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, competition math benchmarks
  quote: "Muennighoff et al. (2025) curate a dataset of 1,000 samples, emphasizing difficulty, diversity, and quality. Their work demonstrates that fine-tuning Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on this dataset achieves performance surpassing o1-preview on competition math benchmarks."
  where: p.33

- A CoT meta-analysis of 100 papers (Sprague et al. 2024a): CoT helps math, logic and algorithmic tasks and gives minimal gains elsewhere.
  number: 100 papers
  setup: meta-analysis
  quote: "Sprague et al. (2024a) conduct a meta-analysis of 100 CoT papers, showing that CoT significantly improves performance on mathematical, logical, and algorithmic reasoning tasks but offers minimal gains for non-symbolic tasks."
  where: p.38

- Evaluating reasoning is open. A correct answer does not guarantee a sound chain, and chains are often unfaithful. A model that cannot do the task cannot judge it.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 6.2.1
  quote: "if a model cannot perform a task, how can it judge if the task is done correctly?"
  where: p.37

- Multi-agent patterns. Debate has two forms: independent answers plus others' advice (Wang 2024h), or opposing stances (Liang 2023b). Consensus comes via a judge, weighted voting or a fixed number of rounds. ReConcile uses confidence-weighted voting. Mixture-of-Agents chains agents. Magentic-One uses an orchestrator. A central planner is more efficient but is a single point of failure. GroupDebate cuts token cost.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2.3.4, 3.3
  quote: "Compared with decentralized communication, it can lead to more efficient resource allocation but increase the system vulnerability to potential failure of the central node."
  where: p.19

- Open question about agentic reasoning: whether it always helps on simple tasks is debated, and current autonomy is mostly limited to planning. Agents lack proactiveness (they do not ask for clarification).
  number: none
  setup: Sec 6.1.2
  quote: "there is ongoing debate about whether agentic reasoning isalwaysbeneficial, especially for straightforward and simple tasks"
  where: p.34

- Data limits for RL: human-annotated problems are nearly exhausted. Verifiable rewards are hard in open-ended generation, software engineering and most agentic tasks. Process supervision has high annotation cost and is ill-defined in long CoT.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 6.2.3
  quote: "we are nearing the limits of available human-annotated data"
  where: p.39

- Tool and protocol notes. ReAct and LATS (MCTS + ReAct) are the single-agent inference-scaling baselines. MCP gets a short mention, citing Hou et al. 2025 on missing security oversight and weak authentication/authorization.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.2, 3.2.2
  quote: "the absence of centralized security oversight, gaps in authentication and authorization, and difficulties in maintaining consistency across multi-step, cross-system workflows."
  where: p.18

LIMITS
- It is a survey, so there are no experiments of its own and no head-to-head comparisons. Every performance claim is secondhand.
- The authors say they omit reasoning benchmarks on purpose (footnote 1, p.7) and point to Xu 2025d and Besta 2025.
- The authors concede that reasoning is concentrated in math and code, and that generalization is an open question.
- Recency: Figure 1 counts papers only to 2/2025. Anything after the v1 date of April 2025 is thin, apart from some v4 additions (Qin 2025, Liu 2025c, Ke 2025c). Treat "frontier" claims about o1, o3, R1, Deep Research and Manus as dated to early 2025.
- The multi-agent training material (Sec 5.3) leans on older MARL work (Lau 2012, Matta 2019) and is thin for LLM agents.
- Exact figures such as "4K–20K" or "817" come from other papers, so do not cite them as the survey's own findings.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Wei et al. 2022b (CoT); Kojima et al. 2022 (zero-shot CoT); Wang et al. 2023f (self-consistency); Yao et al. 2023a (Tree of Thoughts); Besta et al. 2024 (Graph of Thoughts); Yao et al. 2023b (ReAct); Zhou et al. 2024a (LATS); Madaan et al. 2024 and Saunders et al. 2022 (self-refinement); Snell et al. 2024/2025 (test-time compute); Lightman et al. 2024 (PRM); Schulman et al. 2017 (PPO); Rafailov et al. 2023 (DPO); Shao et al. 2024 (GRPO); DeepSeek-AI et al. 2025 (R1); OpenAI et al. 2024 (o1); Kapoor et al. 2024 (agentic spectrum); Schluntz & Zhang 2024 (workflows); Chen et al. 2023c (ReConcile); Liang et al. 2023b (debate); Wang et al. 2024c (Mixture-of-Agents); Fourney et al. 2024 (Magentic-One); Muennighoff et al. 2025 (s1).

CODE
The survey has no code. These are the formulas worth keeping (the extraction gives them in garbled form, so check the PDF before copying).
- GRPO advantage, Eq. 7, p.22: A = (r_i − mean(R)) / std(R).
- RLOO baseline, Eq. 6, p.22: the leave-one-out mean of the other k−1 rewards.
- DPO loss, Eq. 9, p.23.
- ORM Bradley-Terry loss, Eq. 11, p.24.
- Step-wise PRM loss, Eq. 12, p.24.
- Generative RM loss, Eq. 13: adds −log π(c|x,y) to the SFT or DPO loss.

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p.4): the regime × architecture categorization. It is the single-page map of the whole survey.
- Fig 3 (p.6): taxonomy tree with example papers at each leaf. It works as a reading list.
- Fig 4 (p.9): reasoner, verifier and refiner loop. It is the clearest picture of generator-critic-refiner for note 04.
- Fig 5 (p.10): standalone, single-agent and multi-agent architectures along the agentic spectrum. It makes the agent definition visual.
- Fig 6 (p.12): one tree used for both inference-time selection and training-time preference data. It shows why inference scaling and learning to reason are two uses of the same trajectories.
- Fig 1 (p.2): cumulative reasoning-paper counts 2022 to 2/2025. Low value.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction drops many spaces ("Verifiersthat", "Refinerthat") and mangles equation layout (Eq. 3, 4, 8, 9, 12). The quotes above are verbatim from the extraction, spacing faults included.
- Table 5 (p.21) extracted as a flat list but is readable.
- No embedded instructions found in the text.
- References (pp.40-75) were skimmed only, not read in full.
